paragraphs.en: As cities grow, the distance between the people who eat food and the places where it is grown keeps increasing. Fruit and vegetables often travel long distances before they reach a shop. In response, a growing number of residents, businesses and local authorities are experimenting with urban farming, the practice of producing food within the city itself. Supporters believe that growing food closer to home could reduce transport, provide fresher produce and reconnect city dwellers with nature.

One of the most visible forms is the rooftop garden. Many buildings have flat roofs that are used for nothing at all, and these can be covered with raised beds or containers of soil. Supporters point out that such gardens do more than produce vegetables. A layer of plants can help keep the building beneath cooler in summer and can absorb some of the rainwater that would otherwise rush into drains. Before a garden is created, however, engineers should check whether the roof can carry the extra weight of wet soil.

A more technological approach is the vertical farm. Here, crops are grown indoors on shelves stacked one above another, under artificial lights. Instead of soil, the roots receive water containing nutrients, and the conditions can be controlled so carefully that harvests are possible all year round. Such farms often use much less water than open fields. Their main weakness is cost, since lighting and climate control consume a great deal of electricity. For this reason, they mostly grow leafy greens and herbs rather than staple crops.

Community gardens take a simpler and more social form. A piece of unused land is divided into small plots, and local people grow whatever they like. Gardeners often say that the friendships formed over the fence are as valuable as the tomatoes, and children who take part learn where their food actually comes from. Such gardens can also turn neglected corners of a neighbourhood into pleasant green spaces.

In Uzbekistan, this idea is hardly new. Traditional courtyard houses have long had grapevines, apricot trees and small vegetable beds, and many families still grow part of their own food. Some mahallas are now applying the same tradition on a shared scale, planting fruit trees and vegetables on unused land near schools or apartment blocks. Such projects are often carried out through hashar, the custom of neighbours working together voluntarily for the common good.

Despite the enthusiasm, urban farming has clear limits. Land in cities is expensive, and developers usually prefer to build on it. Soil in former industrial areas may be polluted, so it needs testing before anything edible is planted. Most importantly, city farms produce only a small share of what urban populations eat, and some critics argue that they are closer to a hobby than a real solution. Growing food in a small space also requires time and knowledge, which not every resident has.

Even so, it would be a mistake to judge urban farming only by the amount of food it produces. It can bring neighbours together, make cities greener and teach young people valuable skills. Rather than replacing rural agriculture, it is perhaps best understood as a useful addition to it.
